Integration

An integral adds up a rate. Read as the area under a density, it says how often a −5% day should happen; 0050 says otherwise.

Volume I · Calculus for FinanceBuilds on LM1 · LM2 · LM3Leads to LM12 · LM13 · LM14 · LM15 · LM16 · LM17 · LM18Time ≈ 2.5 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1interpret a definite integral as accumulated change and as signed area, and approximate it with left, right and midpoint Riemann sums
2evaluate definite integrals with the fundamental theorem of calculus, and differentiate integrals whose limits depend on a variable
3apply substitution and integration by parts to the integrals that recur in finance, including the standardization of a normal probability
4determine whether an improper integral converges, derive the Gaussian integral, and explain how a heavy tail makes a variance or kurtosis infinite
5calculate the present value and duration of a continuous cash-flow stream under continuous discounting
6calculate probabilities and expectations as integrals of a density, and compare a normal model's tail probabilities with the observed frequencies of 0050's daily returns
7implement the trapezoidal and Simpson rules, state their error orders, and verify them numerically and with scipy.integrate
Learning Module Overview
  • A definite integral adds up a rate and equals a signed area. Left and right Riemann sums err by O(Δt), midpoint sums by O(Δt2): for a deposit rate rising from 1.5% toward 2%, four quarterly left panels miss the accumulated rate by 5.85 bp, twelve monthly midpoints by 0.025 bp.
  • The fundamental theorem of calculus, ∫ab​f=F(b)−F(a) for any F with F′=f, turns accumulation into antidifferentiation. With Φ′=φ it shows that at 0050's −5% threshold a 1% error in volatility moves the tail probability by about 18%.
  • Substitution reduces every normal probability to one function, Pr(R≤κ)=Φ((κ−μ)/σ). Integration by parts integrates LM2's forward curve back into its yield curve and brackets the normal tail between φ(ω)/ω⋅(1−1/ω2) and φ(ω)/ω.
  • ∫−∞∞​e−x2/2dx=2π​. A power tail x−α−1 keeps only the moments of order below α; with α≈3, as reported for index returns, kurtosis is infinite, and 0050's sample excess kurtosis jumped from 5.84 to 7.63 on 7 April 2025.
  • A continuous stream CF(t) is worth ∫0T​CF(t)e−rtdt; monthly payments are Riemann sums of it. NT$30,000 a month for 20 years at a continuously compounded 2% is worth NT$5,929,295 in arrears, NT$5,939,186 in advance and NT$5,934,239 as a stream, within NT$1 of mid-month payment.
  • A normal model fitted to 0050's 2,902 daily returns gives Pr(R≤−5%)=Φ(−4.1074)=2.0×10−5: 0.058 days in twelve years, one every 206 years. The data contain nine, 155 times as many, and those days averaged −6.54% against the model's −5.27%.
  • If annual log growth is normal with mean μX​ and variance σX2​, the growth factor has median eμX​ and mean eμX​+σX2​/2, exactly. For 0050 the median is 21.30% a year, its realized compound growth, and the mean 23.58%.
  • The normal density has no elementary antiderivative, so Φ has no formula. Halving the step divides the trapezoid rule's error by 4 and Simpson's by 16; on the −5% tail, 256 Simpson panels reach a relative error of 1.2×10−6 and adaptive quadrature a relative 7×10−11.

1Introduction

An integral adds up a quantity that changes continuously: interest accruing under a moving rate, cash arriving as a stream, probability spread along the return axis. Each is a rate multiplied by a small width and summed, and each is the area under a curve. This module builds the integral from such sums, evaluates it with the fundamental theorem of calculus, extends it to infinite intervals and computes it numerically when no formula exists. One risk question runs through all of it.

Motivating CaseHow often should a −5% day happen?

Take 0050's 2,902 daily total returns from 3 November 2014 to 8 October 2026. Their mean is 0.0871% and their standard deviation 1.2385%. A risk model that treats daily returns as normal with these two numbers draws a bell curve. The probability of a day at or below −5% is the area under that curve to the left of −5%.

That area is 2.0×10−5. Over 2,902 days the model expects 0.058 such days, or one every 206 years.

The data contain nine (Exhibit 1). Five of them fell between April 2024 and July 2026. On 7 April 2025 0050 closed down 10.000%, the exchange's daily limit; under the fitted model a day that bad comes once in 2×1013 years.

Was the area computed wrongly, is the model wrong, or was the market unlucky? The area has no formula, because the bell curve has no elementary antiderivative. By Section 8 you will compute it four ways, compare it with the data threshold by threshold, and see where the model's tail runs out.

Sections 2 and 3 define the integral as a limit of sums and evaluate it with antiderivatives; Section 4 adds substitution and integration by parts. Section 5 extends integrals to infinite intervals and shows how heavy tails make moments infinite. Section 6 values continuous cash flows, Section 7 resolves the case with densities, and Sections 8 and 9 compute integrals numerically, by hand and in Python.

NoteNotation in this module

As in LM3, f is a generic function (this module has no exposures) and F an antiderivative, F′=f; u and h are further generic functions, x a generic coordinate, and a and b the ends of an interval [a,b] (this module has no bets). A variable of integration (t, x, u) has a meaning only inside its integral. A density is also an f; φ(z)=e−z2/2/2π​ is the standard normal density, Φ its distribution function, z a standardized value and Pr a probability. X is a generic random quantity with density f, instantiated per example (the Pareto ratio R/κ, the log growth lnG), and Z a standard normal one; X∼N(μ,σ2) says that probabilities of X are areas under the normal density with mean μ and standard deviation σ (LM13 defines random variables).

r is a continuously compounded rate per year, r(t) the instantaneous rate at time t and T a horizon in years. μ^​ and s are the sample mean and population standard deviation of 0050's daily returns; the counts are n=2,902 returns and N panels of width Δt or Δx, i and j are summation indices, and k is a moment's order. Local symbols: the threshold κ; the accumulation function I(x); the sums LN​, RN​, MN​, TN​, SN​ (left, right, midpoint, trapezoid, Simpson), distinct from the return R and the horizon T, and a panel's midpoint m; constants η, ζ; the normal tail Q(ω) beyond ω>0; the cash-flow rate CF(t); the tail index α, power β and Student t degrees of freedom ν; the mean μX​ and variance σX2​ of log growth.

2Accumulation and Area

interpret a definite integral as accumulated change and as signed area, and approximate it with left, right and midpoint Riemann sums

Rate times time, added up

A deposit earning a constant continuously compounded rate r for a time Δt accumulates rΔt of log growth (LM1). If the rate moves during the year, no single product works. Split the year into short pieces on which the rate is nearly constant, multiply each piece's rate by its length, and add. The finer the split, the closer the sum comes to one number: the accumulated rate.

Draw the rate as a curve over the time axis. Each product is a thin rectangle, the sum is the area of a staircase, and the limit is the area under the curve. Accumulation and area are one idea.

DefinitionRiemann sum and definite integral

For f defined on [a,b], choose a partition a=t0​<t1​<⋯<tN​=b with widths Δti​=ti​−ti−1​ and a sample point ξi​∈[ti−1​,ti​] in each piece. The Riemann sum is ∑i=1N​f(ξi​)Δti​. The function f is integrable on [a,b] if these sums approach one number as the widest piece shrinks to zero, whatever the sample points. That number is the definite integral

∫ab​f(t)dt:=maxi​Δti​→0lim​ i=1∑N​f(ξi​)Δti​.(5.1)

Every continuous function on a closed interval is integrable. So is a bounded function with finitely many jumps, such as a policy rate that changes on announcement dates (stated without proof; Stewart, Clegg and Watson 2021). The letter t is a dummy: ∫ab​f(t)dt=∫ab​f(x)dx.

Where f is negative the products are negative, so the integral is a signed area: area above the axis minus area below. A P&L rate that is positive in the morning and negative in the afternoon integrates to the day's net P&L, not its gross. Three properties follow at once from the same properties of finite sums:

  • Linearity: ∫ab​(ηf+ζh)=η∫ab​f+ζ∫ab​h for constants η, ζ.
  • Additivity: ∫ab​f=∫ax0​​f+∫x0​b​f for x0​∈[a,b]; we set ∫ba​f:=−∫ab​f.
  • Monotonicity: if f≤h on [a,b] then ∫ab​f≤∫ab​h; in particular fmin​(b−a)≤∫ab​f≤fmax​(b−a) when fmin​≤f≤fmax​.

Left, right and midpoint sums

With N equal panels of width Δt=(b−a)/N and grid points ti​=a+iΔt, three choices of sample point have names:

LN​=Δti=0∑N−1​f(ti​),RN​=Δti=1∑N​f(ti​),MN​=Δti=1∑N​f(ti​−2Δt​).

For an increasing f the left value of each panel is its minimum and the right value its maximum, so LN​≤∫ab​f≤RN​. The gap telescopes:

RN​−LN​=Δti=1∑N​[f(ti​)−f(ti−1​)]=Δt[f(b)−f(a)].

So for a monotone function each one-sided sum lies within Δt∣f(b)−f(a)∣ of the integral. The error is O(Δt): halving the panel width halves the error bound. The midpoint sum does much better, with an error of order Δt2; Section 8 shows why.

Example 1Accruing a rising deposit rate

A one-year floating-rate deposit is expected to pay the continuously compounded rate r(t)=2.0%−0.5%e−2t, with t in years (an illustrative path, not a forecast). The rate starts at 1.5% and approaches 2.0%. Approximate the accumulated rate ∫01​r(t)dt with left, right and midpoint sums for N=4, 12 and 365, and value NT$1,000,000 deposited for the year.

Solution

For N=4, Δt=0.25 and the rate at t=0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1 is 1.50000%, 1.69673%, 1.81606%, 1.88843% and 1.93233%. The left sum is 0.25×(1.50000+1.69673+1.81606+1.88843)%=1.7253%; the right sum drops the first rate and adds the last, giving 1.8334%. The exact value, 1.7838%, comes from Section 3 in one line. Exhibit 2 draws both staircases.

Panels N Left LN​ Right RN​ Midpoint MN​
4 1.7253% (−5.85 bp) 1.8334% (+4.96 bp) 1.7861% (+0.224 bp)
12 1.7653% (−1.85 bp) 1.8013% (+1.75 bp) 1.7841% (+0.0250 bp)
365 1.7832% (−0.0593 bp) 1.7844% (+0.0592 bp) 1.7838% (+0.00003 bp)

Errors, sum minus exact value, computed before rounding, are in brackets. Moving from 4 to 12 panels makes Δt three times smaller: the one-sided errors shrink about threefold, as O(Δt) predicts, and the midpoint error about ninefold, as O(Δt2) predicts. At N=4 both one-sided errors respect the bound Δt[r(1)−r(0)]=0.25×0.43233%=10.8 bp.

In money: the exact accumulation factor is e0.01783834=1.017998, so NT$1,000,000 grows to NT$1,017,998. The quarterly left sum predicts NT$1,017,403, NT$596 short (computed before rounding), and the quarterly midpoint sum NT$1,018,021. Daily accrual, N=365, is itself a Riemann sum, and its left-sum error is under 0.06 bp.

PitfallRates per year, time in days

An integral of a rate is only meaningful when t is measured in the unit of the rate's denominator. A 2% annual rate held for 30 calendar days accrues 0.02×30/365=0.164% of log growth, not 0.02×30. Convert the time axis, not the answer, and decide whether a year means 365 calendar days or A=243.1 trading days, as in the case's sample (LM1).

導讀積分就是「累積」

速率乘以時間就是累積量：利率乘以期間得到利息，機率密度乘以區間寬度得到機率。速率會變動時，就把區間切細，每一小段用「當時的速率 × 寬度」近似，再全部加總，這就是黎曼和；切到無限細的極限就是定積分，也就是曲線下的有號面積。左端點與右端點近似的誤差與格寬 Δt 成正比，中點近似的誤差與 Δt2 成正比，所以中點法收斂快得多。銀行的「每日計息」本身就是一個 Δt=1/365 的黎曼和。

Knowledge Check 1

A rate path falls steadily (monotonically) from 2.0% to 1.5% over one year. Does the left sum L4​ overestimate or underestimate ∫01​r(t)dt? Bound its error using only the two endpoint rates.

Answer

For a decreasing function each panel's left value is its maximum, so L4​ overestimates and R4​ underestimates. The telescoping argument gives ∣L4​−∫01​r∣≤Δt∣r(1)−r(0)∣=0.25×0.5%=12.5 bp.

3The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

evaluate definite integrals with the fundamental theorem of calculus, and differentiate integrals whose limits depend on a variable

Riemann sums define the integral but are a slow way to compute it. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects integrals with the derivatives of LM2: accumulating a rate and differentiating an accumulated amount undo each other.

Define the accumulation function I(x):=∫ax​f(t)dt. Increase x by a small Δx: I gains a thin strip of width Δx whose height is close to f(x), so I(x+Δx)−I(x)≈f(x)Δx. The rate at which accumulated area grows is the height of the curve.

TheoremFundamental theorem of calculus

Let f be continuous on [a,b].

  1. The accumulation function I(x):=∫ax​f(t)dt is differentiable on (a,b), with I′(x)=f(x).
  2. If F is any function with F′=f on [a,b], an antiderivative of f, then
    ∫ab​f(t)dt=F(b)−F(a)=:[F(t)]ab​.(5.2)

Proof. (1) For Δx>0 let fmin​ and fmax​ be the minimum and maximum of f on [x,x+Δx]. Additivity and monotonicity give fmin​Δx≤I(x+Δx)−I(x)≤fmax​Δx; divide by Δx. As Δx→0, continuity squeezes fmin​ and fmax​ to f(x), so the difference quotient tends to f(x); the case Δx<0 is symmetric.

(2) By part 1, I−F has zero derivative on (a,b), so it is constant there by the mean value theorem (LM2), and by continuity on [a,b]. Since I(a)=0, I(x)=F(x)−F(a), and x=b gives (5.2). ■

Part 2 is the computing tool: find any antiderivative and subtract. Two antiderivatives differ by a constant, which cancels. The family of all antiderivatives is the indefinite integral, written ∫f(t)dt=F(t)+C. Every derivative rule of LM2 read backwards is an antiderivative; Exhibit 3 lists the ones this book uses.

Accumulation with a moving rate

The theorem finishes Example 1 exactly. An antiderivative of 2.0%−0.5%e−2t is 2.0%t+0.25%e−2t, so ∫01​r(t)dt=2.0%+0.25%(e−2−1)=1.783834%.

More generally, money compounding at a moving rate satisfies W′(t)=r(t)W(t): it grows at the rate r(t) per unit of wealth. By the chain rule (lnW)′=W′/W=r(t), so lnW is an antiderivative of r, and (5.2) gives

W(T)=W(0)exp(∫0T​r(t)dt),P(T)=exp(−∫0T​r(t)dt).(5.3)

P(T) is the discount factor for time T. With a constant rate, (5.3) is the erT of LM1; with a moving rate, the integral replaces rT. The average rate y(T):=T1​∫0T​r(t)dt is the continuously compounded zero yield, and r(T) is the forward rate of LM2, as Section 4 confirms.

Limits that move

Part 1 combined with the chain rule differentiates integrals whose limits depend on a variable. If u and h are differentiable and f is continuous on an interval containing their values,

dxd​∫h(x)u(x)​f(t)dt=f(u(x))u′(x)−f(h(x))h′(x).

The case that matters most here is the normal distribution function Φ(z):=∫−∞z​φ(t)dt, the area to the left of z under the standard normal density. Section 5 shows that this area is finite. Writing Φ(z)=Φ(0)+∫0z​φ(t)dt and applying part 1 gives Φ′(z)=φ(z).

Example 2How sensitive is a tail probability to volatility?

Under a normal model with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the probability of a day at or below κ is Φ(z) with z=(κ−μ)/σ; Section 4 derives this. For the case, κ=−5%, μ=μ^​=0.0871% and σ=s=1.2385%; at full precision (Example 3) they give z=−4.1074386, where φ(z)=8.6578×10−5 and Φ(z)=2.0004×10−5 (Section 7 computes φ, Section 8 Φ). Find the elasticity (σ/Φ)dΦ(z)/dσ, and compare its linear prediction for a 10% higher σ with the exact change.

Solution

The chain rule and Φ′=φ give dΦ(z)/dσ=φ(z)dz/dσ with dz/dσ=−(κ−μ)/σ2=−z/σ. The elasticity is therefore −zφ(z)/Φ(z)=4.1074386×4.328=17.78. A 1% error in σ moves the tail probability by about 18%.

For σ 10% higher, 1.3624%, the linear prediction is +178%. Exactly, z becomes −4.1074386/1.1=−3.73404 and Φ(z)=9.422×10−5, 4.71 times the original: +371%. The linear rule ignores compounding: an elasticity converts small percentage changes, and over a 10% move they compound.

Even in logs, 17.78×ln1.1=1.6946, a factor of 5.44, overshoots, because the elasticity falls to 14.83 at the new z. Under a normal model a 10% error in σ is almost a factor-of-five error in the probability of a −5% day.

PitfallThe theorem needs continuity on the whole interval

Applied blindly, (5.2) gives ∫−11​x−2dx=[−1/x]−11​=−2: a negative area for a positive function. The integrand is unbounded at 0, so the integral is improper (Section 5); each half diverges, and the integral does not exist. Check that f is continuous on the closed interval before subtracting antiderivative values.

導讀微積分基本定理：累積與速率互為逆運算

把速率從 a 累積到 x 得到累積函數 I(x)，再對 I 微分，就回到原本的速率 f(x)。所以算定積分不必真的加總無限多個長方形，只要找到任何一個導數等於 f 的函數 F，計算 F(b)−F(a) 即可。利率會變動時，財富是 W(T)=W(0)exp(∫0T​r)，積分取代了 rT。同一個定理也說常態分布函數的導數就是密度，Φ′=φ，由此可知尾端機率對波動度極為敏感：在 −5% 的門檻，σ 錯 10%，機率就差將近 5 倍。

Knowledge Check 2

LM2 defined the instantaneous forward rate as −dTd​lnP(T). Show that this definition agrees with (5.3).

Answer

From (5.3), lnP(T)=−∫0T​r(t)dt. By part 1 of the theorem, −dTd​lnP(T)=r(T): the forward rate of LM2 is exactly the integrand of (5.3). A rate curve and its discount curve carry the same information; differentiation and integration convert one into the other.

4Techniques: Substitution and Integration by Parts

apply substitution and integration by parts to the integrals that recur in finance, including the standardization of a normal probability

Most antiderivatives in finance come from two rules, each a derivative rule of LM2 read backwards. The chain rule becomes substitution; the product rule becomes integration by parts.

Substitution

If F′=f, the chain rule gives dxd​F(u(x))=f(u(x))u′(x). Integrating both sides with (5.2) gives the rule.

ResultSubstitution rule

If u has a continuous derivative on [a,b] and f is continuous on an interval containing u([a,b]), then

∫ab​f(u(x))u′(x)dx=∫u(a)u(b)​f(u)du.(5.4)

In practice: name the inner function u, replace u′(x)dx by du, and move the limits with the variable. The bookkeeping “du=u′(x)dx” is the chain rule.

Standardizing. The substitution that matters most here is linear. The normal density with mean μ and standard deviation σ is f(x)=σ1​φ(σx−μ​). With u=(x−μ)/σ we have du=dx/σ, and (5.4) gives

∫ab​σ1​φ(σx−μ​)dx=∫(a−μ)/σ(b−μ)/σ​φ(u)du=Φ(σb−μ​)−Φ(σa−μ​).(5.5)

Every normal probability is a difference of two values of one function, Φ. The factor 1/σ is not decoration: stretching the horizontal axis by σ must shrink the height by σ, or the area would change. Letting a→−∞, which Section 5 justifies, gives Pr(R≤κ)=Φ((κ−μ)/σ).

Example 3The −5% question as one number

Under the case's normal model, express Pr(R≤−5%) and Pr(−1%<R≤1%) through Φ, and compare the second with the data.

Solution

For the tail, with μ^​ and s carried to full precision, z=(−0.05−0.000871205)/0.0123851406=−4.1074386, so Pr(R≤−5%)=Φ(−4.1074386): a −5% day is a “4.1-sigma” day for 0050. The sample standard deviation with divisor n−1, 1.23873%, gives z=−4.1067 and a probability 0.3% higher, which changes none of the conclusions.

For the centre, the limits standardize to (−0.01−0.000871)/0.012385=−0.878 and (0.01−0.000871)/0.012385=0.737. So Pr=Φ(0.737)−Φ(−0.878)=0.769−0.190=0.579. In the data, 2,029 of the 2,902 days, 69.92%, fell in that band.

The normal model puts too little probability near zero as well as in the far tails. It compensates in the shoulders: between −3% and −1% (−3%<R≤−1%) it expects 533 days against 352 observed, and between +1% and +3% (1%<R≤3%) it expects 642 against 434.

A non-linear substitution. With u=−x2/2 and du=−xdx,

∫xe−x2/2dx=−∫eudu=−e−x2/2+C,so∫zφ(z)dz=−φ(z)+C.

This identity gives the normal model's tail means in Section 7 and the polar-coordinates proof in Section 5.

Integration by parts

The product rule (uh)′=u′h+uh′, integrated with (5.2), trades one integral for another.

ResultIntegration by parts

If u and h have continuous derivatives on [a,b], then

∫ab​u(x)h′(x)dx=[u(x)h(x)]ab​−∫ab​u′(x)h(x)dx.(5.6)

The trade pays when u becomes simpler on differentiation, such as a power of t, while h′ is easy to integrate, such as an exponential.

Time-weighted discounting. Take u=t and h′=e−rt, so h=−e−rt/r:

∫0T​te−rtdt=[−rt​e−rt]0T​+r1​∫0T​e−rtdt=r21−(1+rT)e−rT​.

The integrand weights each instant's discount factor by its date; Section 6 turns the integral into a duration. The Deep Dive of LM3 used the same rule to derive the integral form of Taylor's remainder.

Example 4Integrating LM2's forward curve back into its yield curve

LM2 differentiated the illustrative zero-yield curve y(T)=2.0%−0.8%e−T/3 and obtained the forward rate y(T)+Ty′(T). Written as a function of t, the forward curve is r(t)=2.0%−0.8%e−t/3(1−t/3). Integrate it from 0 to T, show that the result equals Ty(T), and compute the discount factors for T=1, 5 and 10.

Solution

Split the integral: ∫0T​r(t)dt=2.0%T−0.8%∫0T​e−t/3dt+30.8%​∫0T​te−t/3dt. The first integral is 3(1−e−T/3). For the second, (5.6) with u=t and h=−3e−t/3 gives ∫0T​te−t/3dt=−3Te−T/3+9(1−e−T/3).

Collecting terms, −2.4%(1−e−T/3) and +2.4%(1−e−T/3) cancel, leaving ∫0T​r(t)dt=2.0%T−0.8%Te−T/3=Ty(T).

T ∫0T​te−t/3dt ∫0T​r(t)dt y(T) P(T)=e−∫0T​r
1 0.401624 0.0142677 1.42677% 0.985834
5 4.466986 0.0924450 1.84890% 0.911699
10 7.608714 0.1971461 1.97146% 0.821071

The yields match LM2's table. Differentiating took LM2 one product rule; undoing it takes one integration by parts. The yield is the average forward rate, as (5.3) says.

PitfallSubstituting without moving the limits or the factor 1/σ

Drop the 1/σ in (5.5) and the “probability” of the whole real line becomes σ, 0.012 for 0050. Substitute u=(x−μ)/σ but keep the old limit −0.05, and you compute Φ(−0.05)=0.48 instead of Φ(−4.107)=2.0×10−5. In a definite integral the limits are values of the integration variable, so they change with it.

導讀兩個技巧：連鎖律與乘積律倒著用

變數變換是連鎖律倒過來：把內層函數叫做 u，u′(x)dx 換成 du，上下限也要跟著換成 u 的值。最重要的例子是標準化 z=(x−μ)/σ，任何常態機率都變成同一個函數 Φ 的差，而 1/σ 這個因子確保面積不變。分部積分是乘積律倒過來，適合「一個因子微分後變簡單、另一個因子容易積分」的情形，例如 te−rt。把 LM2 的遠期利率曲線用分部積分積回去，就得到原本的殖利率曲線：殖利率就是遠期利率的平均。

Knowledge Check 3

Show that under the normal model Pr(R>κ)=Φ((μ−κ)/σ), and evaluate it for κ=+5% with the case's parameters.

Answer

Pr(R>κ)=1−Φ((κ−μ)/σ). Because φ is symmetric, the area right of z equals the area left of −z. Once Section 5 shows that the total area is 1, this gives 1−Φ(z)=Φ(−z). With z=(0.05−0.000871)/0.012385=3.9668, Pr=Φ(−3.9668)=3.64×10−5: 0.106 expected days, against 6 in the data (Practice Problem 15).

5Improper Integrals and the Gaussian Integral

determine whether an improper integral converges, derive the Gaussian integral, and explain how a heavy tail makes a variance or kurtosis infinite

Tail probabilities, perpetuities and moments integrate over unbounded intervals. Definition (5.1) needs a bounded interval and a bounded integrand, so we extend it with a limit.

DefinitionImproper integral

If f is integrable on [a,b] for every b>a, then ∫a∞​f(x)dx:=limb→∞​∫ab​f(x)dx. The integral converges if the limit exists and is finite, and diverges otherwise; ∫−∞b​f is defined in the same way. If f is unbounded near a, then ∫ab​f:=limε↓0​∫a+εb​f. A two-sided integral ∫−∞∞​f converges if ∫−∞0​f and ∫0∞​f both converge, and its value is their sum.

Power functions are the benchmark.

PropositionPower test

∫1∞​x−βdx converges if and only if β>1, and then equals 1/(β−1). ∫01​x−βdx converges if and only if β<1.

Proof. For β=1, ∫1b​x−βdx=(b1−β−1)/(1−β), which tends to 1/(β−1) if β>1 and to ∞ if β<1. For β=1 the integral is lnb→∞. The second statement follows in the same way from ∫ε1​x−βdx as ε↓0. ■

So 1/x is the dividing line: ∫1∞​x−2dx=1, but ∫1∞​x−1dx=∞, although both integrands go to zero. Exponentials decay faster than any power. For r>0, ∫0∞​e−rtdt=limb→∞​(1−e−rb)/r=1/r, the value of a perpetuity paying 1 a year (Section 6).

PropositionComparison test

If 0≤f(x)≤h(x) for x≥a and ∫a∞​h converges, then ∫a∞​f converges. If ∫a∞​f diverges, so does ∫a∞​h.

The reason: I(b)=∫ab​f never decreases as b grows and never exceeds ∫a∞​h. A non-decreasing bounded function has a finite limit, a property of the real numbers that we state without proof.

The Gaussian integral

The bell curve e−x2/2 has no elementary antiderivative, yet its total area is known exactly. It is finite: (∣x∣−1)2≥0 gives x2/2≥∣x∣−1/2, so e−x2/2≤e1/2e−∣x∣, whose integral over each half-line converges.

TheoremGaussian integral
∫−∞∞​e−x2/2dx=2π​.(5.7)
Deep DiveProof of the Gaussian integral with polar coordinatesoptional · click to expand

Here x,y are Cartesian coordinates and ρ,θ polar ones, a point's distance from the origin and its angle. Let Jb​:=∫−bb​e−x2/2dx; we need limb→∞​Jb​.

Step 1 (from a square to a double integral). Jb2​=(∫−bb​e−x2/2dx)(∫−bb​e−y2/2dy)=∬[−b,b]2​e−(x2+y2)/2dxdy. A double integral is the limit of Riemann sums over small rectangles. For a continuous function on a rectangle it equals either iterated integral (Fubini's theorem, stated without proof; Stewart, Clegg and Watson 2021). Here the integrand factorizes as e−x2/2e−y2/2, so the iterated integral is the product of the two one-dimensional integrals.

Step 2 (polar coordinates on a disc). The region between radii ρ and ρ+dρ and angles θ and θ+dθ is nearly a rectangle with sides dρ and ρdθ. Its area is therefore ρdρdθ, with an error of order dρ2dθ that vanishes in the limit. The integrand depends on ρ only, through e−ρ2/2. On the disc of radius b, using the substitution u=−ρ2/2 of Section 4,

∬x2+y2≤b2​e−(x2+y2)/2dxdy=∫02π​∫0b​e−ρ2/2ρdρdθ=2π[−e−ρ2/2]0b​=2π(1−e−b2/2).

Step 3 (squeeze). The disc of radius b lies inside the square [−b,b]2, which lies inside the disc of radius b2​. The integrand is positive, so

2π(1−e−b2/2)≤Jb2​≤2π(1−e−b2).
Both bounds tend to 2π, so Jb​→2π​. The two half-line integrals converge by the comparison above, so the two-sided integral equals limb→∞​Jb​=2π​. ■

The factor ρ in the polar area element is what makes the problem solvable: ρe−ρ2/2 has an elementary antiderivative, while e−x2/2 does not.

Two consequences carry the rest of the module. First, φ(z)=e−z2/2/2π​ has total area 1, so Φ(∞)=1; by symmetry Φ(0)=1/2 and Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z). Second, by (5.5) every normal density φ((x−μ)/σ)/σ has total area 1.

Moments of the normal. For every k the function ∣z∣ke−z2/4 is bounded, because exponentials beat powers. So ∣z∣kφ(z) is at most a constant times e−z2/4, and every moment ∫zkφ(z)dz converges by comparison. Odd moments vanish by symmetry. For the second moment, (5.6) with u=z and h′=zφ(z), so that h=−φ(z) by Section 4, gives

∫−∞∞​z2φ(z)dz=[−zφ(z)]−∞∞​+∫−∞∞​φ(z)dz=0+1=1.

So φ has mean 0 and variance 1. By (5.5), the density φ((x−μ)/σ)/σ has mean μ and variance σ2, which is why fitting a normal means matching the sample mean and standard deviation.

Tails that make moments infinite

The normal tail falls like e−x2/2, faster than any power, so every moment is finite. A density whose tail falls only like a power behaves differently. The Pareto density with tail index α>0,

f(x)=αx−α−1for x≥1(and 0 below 1),

integrates to 1 by the power test. Its kth moment is ∫1∞​xkαx−α−1dx=α∫1∞​xk−α−1dx, which by the power test converges if and only if k<α, with value α/(α−k). By comparison, any density whose tail behaves like a constant times x−α−1 obeys the same rule. The Student-t density with ν degrees of freedom, proportional to (1+x2/ν)−(ν+1)/2, has tails like ∣x∣−(ν+1), so its moments exist only below order ν.

Exhibit 4 lists which moments converge, and empirical work places market returns in its middle rows. Mandelbrot (1963) modelled cotton price changes with stable distributions, whose variance is infinite; Cont (2001) instead puts the tail index of most return series between 2 and 5. Gopikrishnan et al. (1999) estimate α≈3 for index returns, and Gabaix et al. (2003) propose a mechanism. With α≈3 the variance is finite, the fourth moment is infinite and the third sits on the borderline.

Example 5Moments of a cubic power tail

Suppose that on days at or below a threshold κ<0 the ratio X=R/κ follows a Pareto law with α=3: density 3x−4 for x≥1. Here α=3 is an illustrative assumption taken from the studies above.

Compute E[X], E[X2] and the variance. Show that E[X3] and E[X4] are infinite through their integrals up to b=10, 100 and 1,000. Then compare the implied mean return beyond κ=−3% with 0050's data and with the normal model.

Solution

E[X]=3/(3−1)=1.5, E[X2]=3/(3−2)=3 and Var(X)=3−1.52=0.75.

For k=3, ∫1b​x3⋅3x−4dx=3lnb: 6.908, 13.816 and 20.723 for b=10, 100 and 1,000. The integral diverges, slowly. For k=4, ∫1b​3dx=3(b−1): 27, 297 and 2,997. It diverges fast.

The model's mean return on days beyond κ is 1.5κ, or −4.50% for κ=−3%. On 0050 the 37 days at or below −3% averaged −4.42%, while the normal model's value from (5.11) in Section 7 is −3.40%. At this threshold the power tail describes the data far better than the normal.

At κ=−5% the Pareto value, −7.50%, is deeper than the data's −6.54%. Nine days are a small sample, and the daily price limit caps moves at 10%. The Taiwan Stock Exchange raised that limit from 7% to 10% on 1 June 2015.

PitfallA sample kurtosis that never settles

Excess kurtosis is kurtosis minus 3, zero for the normal; the sample version uses μ^​ and s (LM19). 0050's sample excess kurtosis over the 2,902 days is 8.12. Without the single day of 7 April 2025 it is 7.05; without the four largest moves, two down and two up, it is 3.85. On the eve of 7 April 2025 the estimate stood at 5.84, and that one day lifted it to 7.63.

The ten largest of the 2,902 terms supply 62.8% of ∑(R−μ^​)4 but only 14.1% of ∑(R−μ^​)2. If the tail index is near 3, the population fourth moment is a divergent integral and no sample is long enough for its estimate to settle. Quote a kurtosis together with its sample period, and prefer tail measures that need fewer moments (LM15, LM32).

導讀瑕積分：尾巴決定動差存不存在

積分區間延伸到無窮遠時用極限來定義，極限存在而且有限才叫收斂。判斷的基準是冪函數：∫1∞​x−βdx 只有在 β>1 時有限，而指數函數衰減得比任何冪函數都快。常態分布的尾巴是 e−x2/2，所以各階動差都存在；尾巴若只像 x−α−1 那樣以冪次衰減（厚尾），就只有低於 α 階的動差存在。文獻估計指數報酬的 α≈3，變異數存在，四階動差（峰態）卻是無窮大，樣本峰態因此永遠穩定不下來。0050 光是 2025/4/7 一天，就讓樣本超額峰態從 5.84 跳到 7.63。

Knowledge Check 4

A Student-t density with ν=3 is symmetric about 0. Which of its mean, variance, third moment and kurtosis exist? Is its third moment zero by symmetry?

Answer

Moments exist below order 3, so the mean (0) and the variance exist and the kurtosis is infinite. The third moment does not exist: ∫∣x∣3f(x)dx diverges like ∫dx/x. That ∫−bb​x3f(x)dx=0 for every b does not help. The two half-line integrals are +∞ and −∞, and a two-sided integral exists only if both halves converge.

6Continuous Discounting and Continuous Cash Flows

calculate the present value and duration of a continuous cash-flow stream under continuous discounting

Section 3's accumulation formula has a mirror image: discounting a stream of cash flows. Discrete payments form geometric series, which LM6 sums. Here payments arrive continuously, or so often that a continuous stream is the simpler model.

A stream pays at the rate CF(t) NT$ per year. Over a short interval [t,t+Δt] it pays about CF(t)Δt, worth CF(t)Δte−rt today at a continuously compounded rate r. Summing over a partition of [0,T] gives a Riemann sum, and in the limit

PV=∫0T​CF(t)e−rtdt,FV=∫0T​CF(t)er(T−t)dt=erTPV.(5.8)

With a moving rate, replace e−rt by the discount factor P(t) of (5.3).

Example 6Monthly rent versus a continuous stream

A property pays NT$30,000 a month for 20 years. Discount at 2% a year, continuously compounded (an illustrative rate). Value the rent (a) paid at the end of each month, (b) paid at the start of each month, (c) paid in mid-month, and (d) modelled as a continuous stream of NT$360,000 a year.

Solution

(d) By Exhibit 5, PV=360,000×(1−e−0.4)/0.02=360,000×16.483998= NT$5,934,239.

(a)–(c) are sums of 240 terms 30,000e−0.02tj​ over the payment dates tj​, geometric series that LM6 sums in closed form. Payment in arrears is worth NT$5,929,295, in advance NT$5,939,186 and in mid-month NT$5,934,238.

Each discrete stream is a Riemann sum of the integral (5.8) with Δt=1/12. Payment in arrears is the right-endpoint rule, in advance the left-endpoint rule and mid-month the midpoint rule. The one-sided sums miss the integral by −NT$4,944 and +NT$4,947 (sum minus integral), about ±0.083%≈±rΔt/2, the leading O(Δt) error. The mid-month stream falls short by less than NT$1 (NT$0.69), an O(Δt2) error.

A continuous stream approximates frequent payments well only if you know where the payments sit. Rent paid in advance is worth 0.167% more than rent paid in arrears.

Duration of a stream

The present-value-weighted average date of a stream is its Macaulay duration,

DMac​:=∫0T​CF(t)e−rtdt∫0T​tCF(t)e−rtdt​.

For a level stream the numerator is CF0​ times Section 4's time-weighted integral, so

DMac​=r(1−e−rT)1−(1+rT)e−rT​=r1​−erT−1T​.

As T→∞, DMac​→1/r: a perpetuity discounted at 2.5% has a duration of 40 years. Differentiating PV(r) under the integral sign gives PV′(r)=−∫0T​tCF(t)e−rtdt, so −PV′(r)/PV(r)=DMac​. This step is permitted because the integrand and its derivative in r are continuous on [0,T] (stated without proof). Under continuous compounding, modified and Macaulay duration coincide; with annual compounding they differ by the factor 1+y of LM2.

PitfallMixing compounding conventions

The formulas of Exhibit 5 need a continuously compounded rate. Convert an effective annual rate first (LM1): an effective 2% is a continuously compounded r=ln1.02=1.9803%. Plugging 2% straight in values Example 6's stream at NT$5,934,239 instead of NT$5,945,187. The NT$10,948 error exceeds the whole gap, about NT$9,900, between rent in advance and rent in arrears.

導讀連續現金流：把年金變成積分

每一小段時間 Δt 收到 CF(t)Δt，折現後加總就是黎曼和，取極限就是 ∫0T​CF(t)e−rtdt。反過來看，每月付款的年金就是這個積分的黎曼和：月底付（後付）是右端點法，月初付（預付）是左端點法，誤差都約是 rΔt/2，月中付是中點法，誤差只有 O(Δt2)，20 年的租金差不到新台幣 1 元。存續期間是以現值加權的平均時間，連續複利下它剛好等於 −PV′(r)/PV，所以修正存續期間與麥考利存續期間相同。成長型永續年金收斂的條件 r>g，就是瑕積分收斂的條件。

Knowledge Check 5

Compute the duration of the continuous stream in Example 6 (T=20, r=2%). Why is it below 10 years?

Answer

DMac​=1/0.02−20/(e0.4−1)=50−40.665=9.335 years. An undiscounted level stream would have its average date at the midpoint, 10 years; discounting gives early payments more weight and pulls the average forward.

7Densities and Expectations

calculate probabilities and expectations as integrals of a density, and compare a normal model's tail probabilities with the observed frequencies of 0050's daily returns

A risk model assigns probabilities to ranges of returns. When a return can take any value in a range, each single value has probability zero. Probability is then spread along the axis with a density, as interest was spread along the time axis in Section 2: probabilities become areas, and averages become integrals. This section defines only what the case needs; LM13 and LM14 build probability theory properly.

DefinitionDensity, distribution function, expectation

A probability density is a function f≥0 with ∫−∞∞​f(x)dx=1. A quantity X has density f if Pr(a<X≤b)=∫ab​f(x)dx for all a<b. Its distribution function is F(x):=Pr(X≤x)=∫−∞x​f(t)dt, and a median of X is a value x with F(x)=1/2. For a function h with ∫∣h(x)∣f(x)dx<∞, the expectation of h(X) is

E[h(X)]:=∫−∞∞​h(x)f(x)dx.(5.9)
In particular the mean is μ=E[X] and the variance σ2=E[(X−μ)2].

By the fundamental theorem, F′=f wherever f is continuous: the density is the rate at which probability accumulates. Definition (5.9) is the limit of the probability-weighted averages ∑i​h(xi​)Pr(xi−1​<X≤xi​), which are Riemann sums. Linearity of the integral makes expectation linear, E[ηX+ζ]=ηE[X]+ζ. When the integral in (5.9) diverges, the expectation does not exist, as for the heavy tails of Section 5.

The case's normal model is R∼N(μ,σ2), with density φ((x−μ)/σ)/σ, mean μ and variance σ2 (Section 5). Fitting it to 0050 sets μ=μ^​=0.0871% and σ=s=1.2385%, the sample mean and population standard deviation; LM20 shows that this is the maximum-likelihood choice.

Bracketing a normal tail by parts

Pr(R≤−5%)=Φ(−4.1074386) has no formula, but integration by parts brackets it. For ω>0 let Q(ω):=1−Φ(ω)=∫ω∞​φ(t)dt, which equals Φ(−ω) by symmetry. Write φ(t)=t1​⋅tφ(t) and apply (5.6) with u=1/t and h=−φ(t), using (−φ)′=tφ:

Q(ω)=[−tφ(t)​]ω∞​−∫ω∞​t2φ(t)​dt=ωφ(ω)​−∫ω∞​t2φ(t)​dt.

The remaining integral is positive, so Q(ω)<φ(ω)/ω. The same step applied to that integral, with u=1/t3, gives ∫ω∞​φ(t)t−2dt=φ(ω)/ω3−3∫ω∞​φ(t)t−4dt<φ(ω)/ω3. Together,

ωφ(ω)​(1−ω21​)<1−Φ(ω)<ωφ(ω)​(ω>0).(5.10)

The two bounds differ by the relative amount 1/ω2, so for large ω the tail is ≈φ(ω)/ω, with a relative error below 1/ω2. Gordon (1941) sharpened the lower bound to φ(ω)/(ω+1/ω). The ratio Q(ω)/φ(ω) is called Mills' ratio. The normal tail shrinks like e−ω2/2/ω, so each extra standard deviation divides it by a factor that itself keeps growing.

Example 7How often should a −5% day happen?

Use (5.10) to bracket Pr(R≤−5%) under the case's normal model and compare the bracket with the exact value. Convert the probability into an expected number of days in the sample and a return period in years.

Solution

From Example 3, Pr(R≤−5%)=Φ(−ω)=Q(ω) with ω=4.1074386. The density there is φ(ω)=8.6578×10−5. Dividing by ω gives the upper bound 2.1078×10−5; multiplying that by 1−1/ω2=0.94073 gives the lower bound 1.9829×10−5. The exact value, computed in Section 8, is 2.0004×10−5: the upper bound is 5.4% high and the lower bound 0.9% low.

Over n=2,902 days the model expects 2,902×2.0004×10−5=0.0581 days. At A=243.1 trading days a year it predicts one such day every 1/(243.1×2.0004×10−5)=205.6 years. The data contain 9, one every 1.33 years: 155 times the model's count. The integral is right; the density is wrong.

Exhibit 6 repeats the comparison at every whole-percent threshold, and Exhibit 7 draws it on a logarithmic axis.

Three features stand out. First, the gap grows explosively with the threshold: the data exceed the model 2.0 times at −3%, 12.8 times at −4% and 155 times at −5%. At −7% three actual days face an expectation of 0.000015.

Second, the model over-predicts moderate losses: 133 days at or below −2% against 104. With Example 3, this gives the data more mass near zero and in the far tails, and less in the shoulders. That is the shape of high kurtosis (Section 5).

Third, a density with a power tail tracks the data. The Student-t with ν=3 and the same standard deviation expects 89.3, 33.2, 15.4 and 8.3 days at −2% to −5%, against 104, 37, 18 and 9. Choosing ν after seeing the data is illustration, not estimation: LM15 fits tail models and LM20 estimates ν.

Example 8The average day beyond −5%

Derive the normal model's mean return on days at or below a threshold κ, E[R∣R≤κ]:=∫−∞κ​xf(x)dx/Pr(R≤κ), and evaluate it at κ=−5% for 0050. Compare it with the nine actual days.

Solution

Substitute x=μ+σu (Section 4), with z=(κ−μ)/σ: ∫−∞κ​xf(x)dx=∫−∞z​(μ+σu)φ(u)du=μΦ(z)+σ∫−∞z​uφ(u)du. Section 4's antiderivative ∫uφ(u)du=−φ(u) makes the last integral −φ(z), since φ vanishes at −∞. Dividing by Φ(z):

E[R∣R≤κ]=μ−σΦ(z)φ(z)​.(5.11)
At z=−4.1074386, φ(z)/Φ(z)=4.328, close to ω+1/ω=4.3509 at ω=−z, as (5.10) suggests. So E[R∣R≤−5%]=0.0871%−1.2385%×4.328=−5.27%.

The nine actual days averaged −6.54%. The normal model misses both how often the tail is reached and how deep the market goes once it is there. The quantity (5.11) is the normal model's conditional tail mean; with κ set at the value-at-risk level, its negative is the expected shortfall of LM32.

Example 9Mean and median of a lognormal growth factor

Suppose the annual log growth X=lnG is normal with mean μX​ and variance σX2​, so that the growth factor G=eX is lognormal. Show that E[G]=eμX​+σX2​/2 and that the median of G is eμX​. Evaluate both with 0050's annualized daily log-return moments, μX​=19.31% and σX​=19.30%.

Solution

By (5.9), E[G]=∫−∞∞​exφ((x−μX​)/σX​)/σX​dx. Complete the square in the exponent:

x−2σX2​(x−μX​)2​=μX​+2σX2​​−2σX2​(x−(μX​+σX2​))2​.
The integrand is therefore eμX​+σX2​/2 times the normal density with mean μX​+σX2​ and variance σX2​, whose integral is 1:
E[G]=E[eX]=eμX​+σX2​/2.(5.12)
For the median: ex is increasing, so Pr(G≤eμX​)=Pr(X≤μX​)=1/2, and the median of G is eμX​.

Annualizing the daily log-return mean and variance with A=243.1 gives μX​=0.19308 and σX2​=0.037265. The median is then e0.19308=1.2130, or +21.30%, and the mean e0.19308+0.018632=1.2358, or +23.58%. The median matches 0050's realized compound growth of 21.30% a year, because the mean daily log return times A is the annualized log growth (LM1). The mean exceeds the median by 2.28 points.

In LM3 the volatility drag RG​≈Rˉ−s2/2 was a second-order approximation; for a lognormal the factor eσX2​/2 between mean and median is exact. The annualization assumes independent daily returns with a constant σ, which this section has just questioned. LM38 derives the same result for geometric Brownian motion.

Pitfall“Sigma” is a statement about a model

“A 4-sigma day” means a probability of Φ(−4)=3.2×10−5 only under a normal model: about once in 130 years of 243.1 trading days. In August 2007 Goldman Sachs's finance chief said: “We were seeing things that were 25-standard deviation moves, several days in a row” (Financial Times, 13 August 2007; quoted by Dowd et al. 2008). Under normality a 25-sigma day has a probability of about 3×10−138. When an “impossible” day recurs, the lesson is that the model's tail is wrong, not that the market was unlucky.

PitfallRaising σ does not fix the tail

To make the normal model expect 9 days at or below −5%, σ must rise to 1.859% a day, 29.0% a year. The same model then expects 379 days at or below −2% (actual 104) and 140 at or below −3% (actual 37). A one-parameter fix moves the whole bell; the data need a different shape. Part of that shape comes from volatility that changes over time (LM26): two of the nine days fell in early 2020, and three in under four months of 2024.

導讀常態模型錯在尾巴的形狀

機率密度是「機率沿著報酬軸分布的速率」，區間機率是面積，期望值是加權積分。用 0050 的平均數與標準差配一條常態曲線，−5% 以下的面積只有 2.0×10−5，12 年預期 0.058 天，約 206 年一次；實際上有 9 天，是模型的 155 倍，而且這幾天平均跌 6.54%，模型只預期 5.27%。問題不在積分算錯，而在密度的形狀：常態尾巴以 e−z2/2 衰減，真實報酬的尾巴比較像冪次衰減，中間也更尖、肩部更少。把 σ 調大救不了：讓 −5% 符合 9 天，−2% 以下就會多估成 379 天。「幾個標準差」的說法只在常態模型下有意義，尾端需要自己的模型（LM15）。

Knowledge Check 6

In Example 2, σ rose 10% to 1.3624%. How many days at or below −5% would that normal model expect in 2,902 days? Does the change close the gap?

Answer

z=−4.1074386/1.1=−3.73404 and Φ(z)=9.422×10−5, so 2,902×9.422×10−5=0.27 days: 4.7 times more than before, but still 33 times short of the 9 observed days. The fragility of Example 2 is real, yet no plausible error in σ explains the data.

8Numerical Integration

implement the trapezoidal and Simpson rules, state their error orders, and verify them numerically and with scipy.integrate

Liouville's theorem rules out a formula for Φ, and integrands defined by data or by other models rarely have one either. A numerical rule replaces the integral by a weighted sum of function values. Its quality lies in its error order: how fast the error falls as the grid is refined.

Three rules

On N panels of width Δx=(b−a)/N, with fi​=f(a+iΔx):

  • Midpoint: MN​=Δx∑i=1N​f(mi​), the height at each panel's midpoint mi​=a+(i−21​)Δx.
  • Trapezoid: TN​=Δx(21​f0​+f1​+⋯+fN−1​+21​fN​)=21​(LN​+RN​), the area under each panel's chord.
  • Simpson (N even): SN​=3Δx​(f0​+4f1​+2f2​+4f3​+⋯+2fN−2​+4fN−1​+fN​), a parabola through each pair of panels.

Error orders from Taylor expansions

Take one panel with midpoint m, from m−Δx/2 to m+Δx/2, and expand f about m (LM3): f(x)=f(m)+f′(m)(x−m)+21​f′′(m)(x−m)2+61​f′′′(m)(x−m)3+O((x−m)4). Integrating over the panel, the odd powers of x−m cancel:

∫m−Δx/2m+Δx/2​f=Δxf(m)+24Δx3​f′′(m)+O(Δx5).

The midpoint rule takes Δxf(m), so its panel error, exact minus rule, is +24Δx3​f′′(m)+O(Δx5). The trapezoid rule takes 2Δx​[f(m−2Δx​)+f(m+2Δx​)]=Δxf(m)+8Δx3​f′′(m)+O(Δx5), so its panel error is −12Δx3​f′′(m)+O(Δx5). Summed over the N panels, ∑i​Δxf′′(mi​) is a midpoint sum for ∫ab​f′′=f′(b)−f′(a), so for f with continuous derivatives up to order four on [a,b]

∫ab​f−TN​≈−12Δx2​[f′(b)−f′(a)],∫ab​f−MN​≈+24Δx2​[f′(b)−f′(a)],(5.13)

with neglected terms of order Δx4. Both rules are O(Δx2): halving Δx divides the error by 4. For f with a continuous second derivative on [a,b], the exact statement ∫ab​f−TN​=−(b−a)Δx2f′′(ξ)/12 for some ξ∈(a,b) is stated without proof (Burden, Faires and Burden 2016, chapter 4).

The two errors in (5.13) have opposite signs and a 2 : 1 ratio, so (2MN​+TN​)/3 cancels the Δx2 term. That combination is Simpson's rule on the 2N half-panels: since T2N​=(TN​+MN​)/2, S2N​=(2MN​+TN​)/3=(4T2N​−TN​)/3. Removing a known leading error term in this way is called Richardson extrapolation. What remains is fourth order: for f with a continuous fourth derivative on [a,b],

∫ab​f−SN​=−180(b−a)Δx4​f(4)(ξ)for some ξ∈(a,b),(5.14)

stated without proof (Burden, Faires and Burden 2016); the Deep Dive derives its leading term. Simpson's rule is therefore O(Δx4): halving Δx divides the error by 16, and the rule is exact for cubic polynomials. Orders bound the worst case. Over the whole real line the trapezoid rule for e−x2/2 overshoots by only 1.3×10−8 at Δx=1, because all its endpoint derivatives vanish at ±∞.

Deep DiveThe leading error term of Simpson's ruleoptional · click to expand

Take a double panel [m−Δx,m+Δx] and expand f about its midpoint m to fourth order. Integrating over the double panel kills the odd powers of x−m:

∫m−Δxm+Δx​f=2Δxf(m)+3Δx3​f′′(m)+60Δx5​f(4)(m)+O(Δx7).
Simpson's rule on this double panel is 3Δx​[f(m−Δx)+4f(m)+f(m+Δx)]. Since f(m−Δx)+f(m+Δx)=2f(m)+Δx2f′′(m)+12Δx4​f(4)(m)+O(Δx6), it equals
2Δxf(m)+3Δx3​f′′(m)+36Δx5​f(4)(m)+O(Δx7).
The Δx and Δx3 terms agree, which is why the rule is exact for cubics. The difference, exact minus rule, is Δx5f(4)(m)(1/60−1/36)=−Δx5f(4)(m)/90. Summing over the (b−a)/(2Δx) double panels, with midpoints mj​, gives −180Δx4​∑j​2Δxf(4)(mj​)≈−180(b−a)Δx4​f(4)(ξ), the leading term of (5.14). ■

Example 10Trapezoid versus Simpson on the −5% tail

Compute Φ(z)=∫−∞z​φ(t)dt numerically for the case's z=−4.1074386. Truncate the lower limit at −12 and bound the truncation error with (5.10). Then apply the trapezoid and Simpson rules with N=8,16,…,1,024 panels and measure the error ratios.

Solution

By (5.10) the part below −12 is Q(12)<φ(12)/12=1.79×10−33; its actual value, 1.78×10−33, is negligible. Exhibit 8 lists the errors against the exact value 2.000355×10−5.

The scale on which φ changes near −4.1 is about 1/4.1=0.24. Once Δx is small against it, the trapezoid ratios settle at 4.00 and Simpson's at 16.0: the O(Δx2) and O(Δx4) of (5.13) and (5.14). At N=256, Δx=7.8925614/256=0.03083. With φ′(t)=−tφ(t) and φ′(−12)=12φ(12)=2.6×10−31, (5.13) predicts T256​−Φ(z)≈+12Δx2​[−zφ(z)]=120.030832​×3.5561×10−4=2.817×10−8 (rule minus exact, as in Exhibit 8), against 2.816×10−8 observed.

With 256 panels the trapezoid rule is still 0.14% high, while Simpson's rule is within a relative 1.2×10−6. On coarse grids neither order is visible: with 16 panels the trapezoid rule is 34% high. As a check on Richardson extrapolation, (4T64​−T32​)/3=2.0009784×10−5=S64​.

Adaptive quadrature

Production code adapts the grid to the integrand. scipy.integrate.quad uses the QUADPACK algorithms (Piessens et al. 1983). On a finite interval it applies a 21-point Gauss–Kronrod rule within subintervals and subdivides adaptively; an infinite range is first mapped onto a finite interval (SciPy documentation). With the case's unrounded z, quad(phi, -inf, z) returns 2.000355×10−5 with an error estimate of 2.2×10−10, within a relative 7×10−11 of the value obtained from the complementary error function.

PitfallError orders are asymptotic

At N=16 the observed ratios in Exhibit 8 are 3.46 and 7.88, not 4 and 16. The orders describe the limit Δx→0, and they appear only once the grid resolves the integrand. Always check by halving Δx: the ratio of successive errors estimates the order and the size of the remaining error, and without an exact value successive differences do the same. A tail integral on a coarse grid can be wrong by a third without any warning.

導讀數值積分：誤差階就是收斂速度

常態密度函數沒有初等的反導函數，所以 Φ 沒有公式，尾端機率一定要用數值方法計算。梯形法用弦取代曲線，中點法取每格中點的高度，兩者誤差都是 O(Δx2)，而且符號相反、大小比 2:1，所以 (2MN​+TN​)/3 會把 Δx2 項消掉，得到 O(Δx4) 的辛普森法，這就是理查森外插。檢查方法很簡單：格寬每減半一次，梯形法誤差應縮小 4 倍、辛普森法 16 倍；比例不對，代表格子還太粗、尚未進入漸近區。實務上可以直接用 scipy.integrate.quad 的自適應積分。

Knowledge Check 7

Simpson's rule with N=8 has an error of 3.2×10−6 on a smooth integrand, and the grid is already in the asymptotic regime. Estimate the error with N=32, and the number of panels needed for an error of 10−10.

Answer

Two halvings divide the error by 162=256: about 1.25×10−8 at N=32. Reaching 10−10 needs a further factor of 125, so (N/32)4=125 and N=32×1251/4=107.0; take N=108, since Simpson's rule needs an even number of panels.

9Integration in Python

implement the trapezoidal and Simpson rules, state their error orders, and verify them numerically and with scipy.integrate

Three habits make numerical integrals trustworthy. Compute a known case alongside the unknown one, halve the step and watch the ratio, and keep data and model in separate, testable functions. quad also integrates (5.8) directly when CF(t) or r(t) has no closed form; the lab values Example 6's stream that way.

Python
import math
import numpy as np
from scipy import integrate, special

def trapezoid(f, a, b, N):    # N panels; error O(dx^2), eq. (5.13)
    x = np.linspace(a, b, N + 1); y = f(x); dx = (b - a) / N
    return dx * (y.sum() - 0.5 * (y[0] + y[-1]))

def simpson(f, a, b, N):      # N even; error O(dx^4), eq. (5.14)
    x = np.linspace(a, b, N + 1); y = f(x); dx = (b - a) / N
    return dx / 3 * (y[0] + y[-1] + 4 * y[1:-1:2].sum() + 2 * y[2:-1:2].sum())

phi = lambda t: np.exp(-0.5 * t * t) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
z = -4.1074386                                  # (kappa - mu_hat) / s at -5%
exact = 0.5 * special.erfc(-z / math.sqrt(2))   # Phi(z) = 2.000355e-05
for N in (64, 128, 256):
    print(N, f"{trapezoid(phi, -12, z, N) - exact:.2e}",
          f"{simpson(phi, -12, z, N) - exact:.2e}")
# 64 4.49e-07 6.23e-09 / 128 1.13e-07 3.94e-10 / 256 2.82e-08 2.47e-11
print("%.6e %.1e" % integrate.quad(phi, -np.inf, z))  # 2.000355e-05 2.2e-10

The data side takes a few lines of Polars, run in labs/LM05_lab. The fitted normal and the count of actual days come from the same series, so Exhibit 6 cannot drift out of sync.

Python
import polars as pl
from scipy import stats
px = pl.read_csv("data/0050_daily_raw.csv")
dv = pl.read_csv("data/0050_dividends.csv").select("date", D="cash_dividend")
days = pl.read_csv("data/00631L_daily_raw.csv").select("date")
c, d = pl.col("close"), pl.col("D").fill_null(0.0)
split = pl.when(pl.col("date") == pl.lit("2025-06-18")).then(4.0).otherwise(1.0)
ret = (px.join(days, on="date", how="semi").join(dv, on="date", how="left")
         .sort("date").with_columns(R=(c + d) / (c.shift(1) / split) - 1)
         .drop_nulls("R"))
mu, s, n = ret["R"].mean(), ret["R"].std(ddof=0), ret.height  # n = 2,902
for kappa in (-0.03, -0.04, -0.05):
    model = n * stats.norm.cdf((kappa - mu) / s)
    # Two-decimal prices make limit moves and round returns exact ties.
    hits = ret.filter(pl.col("R") <= kappa + 1e-12).height  # float guard
    print(f"{kappa:+.0%} normal {model:.3f} actual {hits}")
# -3% normal 18.400 actual 37 / -4% normal 1.403 actual 18
# -5% normal 0.058 actual 9
In PythonCompanion lab

The notebook LM05_lab.ipynb rebuilds the module's computations from the verified FinMind price files. It measures the error orders of Riemann, trapezoid and Simpson sums (Example 1, Exhibit 8). It fits the normal model against 0050's tails (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 6, Exhibit 7), computes the tail means, the lognormal mean and the rent of Example 6, and solves the computational practice problems. It is Polars-first and checks 115 printed numbers.

The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

Summary

  • A definite integral (5.1) is the limit of Riemann sums: accumulated rate times width, or signed area. For monotone integrands the left and right sums err by at most Δt∣f(b)−f(a)∣; the midpoint sum's error is O(Δt2).
  • The fundamental theorem of calculus (5.2) evaluates integrals with antiderivatives and gives dxd​∫ax​f=f(x). Money at a moving rate grows by exp(∫0T​r). Because Φ′=φ, 0050's −5% tail probability moves about 18% per 1% change in σ.
  • Substitution (5.4) reduces every normal probability to Φ through z=(κ−μ)/σ; integration by parts (5.6) handles te−rt, recovers a yield curve from its forward curve, and brackets the normal tail (5.10).
  • Improper integrals are limits. ∫1∞​x−βdx converges only for β>1; ∫e−x2/2dx=2π​ (5.7). A power tail of index α keeps only the moments below order α. With α≈3 kurtosis is infinite, and its sample estimate never settles.
  • A continuous stream is worth ∫0T​CF(t)e−rtdt (5.8). Payments in arrears, in advance and mid-period are right, left and midpoint Riemann sums of that integral. Under continuous compounding, duration equals −PV′/PV.
  • Probabilities and expectations are integrals of a density (5.9). For 0050 the fitted normal gives Pr(R≤−5%)=2.0×10−5, 0.058 expected days against 9 actual, and a tail mean of −5.27% against −6.54%. The lognormal mean is exactly eμX​+σX2​/2 (5.12).
  • The trapezoid and midpoint rules are O(Δx2), Simpson's rule O(Δx4) (5.13–5.14). Halving the step and checking the error ratio is the practical test; adaptive quadrature in scipy.integrate.quad handles infinite ranges.

Practice Problems

  1. The present value of a continuous stream paying 1 a year for 10 years, discounted at a continuously compounded 3%, is closest to:

    • A.8.51
    • B.8.64
    • C.10.00

  2. Compute the left and right sums L4​ and R4​ for ∫01​exdx, the exact value and both errors (sum minus exact). Check the bound Δx[f(b)−f(a)], and compare the average of L4​ and R4​ with (5.13).

  3. dxd​∫0x2​e−t2dt equals:

    • A.2xe−x4
    • B.e−x4
    • C.2xe−x2

  4. Use a substitution to evaluate ∫01​xe−x2/2dx and ∫0∞​xe−x2/2dx.

  5. Show that the Macaulay duration of a continuous perpetuity discounted at r is 1/r, and evaluate it at r=2.5%.

  6. Which integral converges?

    • A.∫1∞​x−1/2dx
    • B.∫01​x−3/2dx
    • C.∫1∞​x−3/2dx

  7. A loss multiple X≥1 has the Pareto density 2.5x−3.5. Compute E[X], E[X2] and Var(X), and state which higher moments are infinite.

  8. A model treats daily returns as normal with μ=0.05% and σ=1.5%. Use (5.10) to bracket Pr(R≤−6%) and compare the bracket with the exact value. Then use the exact value to compute the expected number of such days per year (243.1 trading days) and the return period in years.

  9. Under a normal model, the probability of a day at least four standard deviations below the mean is closest to:

    • A.0.0032%
    • B.0.0063%
    • C.5.9%

  10. A continuous cash flow starts at 1 a year and grows at g=3%; discount at r=5%, both continuously compounded. Compute its 30-year present value, the value of the same stream forever, and the share of the perpetuity's value received in the first 30 years.

  11. Approximate ∫01​e−x2/2dx with T2​, T4​ and S4​, and report the errors (rule minus exact) against the exact value 2π​(Φ(1)−21​)=0.8556244. Show that S4​=(4T4​−T2​)/3.

  12. For a smooth integrand in the asymptotic regime, halving the panel width of Simpson's rule divides its error by a factor closest to:

    • A.4
    • B.8
    • C.16

  13. Annual log growth lnG is normal with mean 8% and standard deviation 20%. Compute the mean and the median of the growth factor G, and Pr(G<1).

  14. Use (5.11) to find E[Z∣Z≤−2] for a standard normal Z.

  15. (Python) With the lab data, count 0050's days with R≥+5%, list their dates, and compare the count with the normal model's expectation.

  16. (Python) Keeping μ^​, find the σ for which the normal model expects exactly 9 days at or below −5%. How many days at or below −2% and −3% does that model then expect?

Solutions

  1. B is correct. (1−e−0.3)/0.03=8.6394. A, 8.5104, pays 1 at each year-end and discounts at the same continuous rate. It is the right-endpoint Riemann sum of the stream, low by about rΔt/2 with Δt=1. C ignores discounting.

  2. With Δx=0.25: L4​=1.512437 (error, sum minus exact, −0.205845), R4​=1.942007 (error +0.223725), exact e−1=1.718282. Both errors are below Δx(e−1)=0.429570 in size. The average T4​=1.727222 errs by +0.008940, close to the overshoot that (5.13) predicts: ∫01​exdx−T4​≈−12Δx2​[f′(1)−f′(0)]=−120.0625​×1.718282=−0.008949. Averaging the one-sided sums turns an O(Δx) error into an O(Δx2) one.

  3. A is correct. By part 1 of the theorem and the chain rule, the derivative is e−(x2)2⋅2x=2xe−x4. B forgets the chain rule; C substitutes the wrong argument.

  4. With u=−x2/2: ∫01​xe−x2/2dx=[−e−x2/2]01​=1−e−1/2=0.3935. As the upper limit grows, e−b2/2→0, so ∫0∞​xe−x2/2dx=1.

  5. Letting T→∞ in Section 4's result gives ∫0∞​te−rtdt=1/r2, and the perpetuity's value is ∫0∞​e−rtdt=1/r. Hence DMac​=(1/r2)/(1/r)=1/r: 40 years at 2.5%.

  6. C is correct. By the power test, ∫1∞​x−3/2dx=1/(3/2−1)=2. A has β=1/2≤1 at infinity; B has β=3/2≥1 near zero. Both diverge.

  7. With α=2.5: E[X]=2.5/1.5=5/3=1.6667, E[X2]=2.5/0.5=5 and Var(X)=5−25/9=2.2222. Moments of order k≥2.5 are infinite, so the third moment, skewness (its standardized form, LM19) and kurtosis do not exist.

  8. z=(−0.06−0.0005)/0.015=−4.03333 and ω=4.03333. Then φ(ω)=1.1706×10−4, the upper bound is φ(ω)/ω=2.9023×10−5 and the lower bound 2.7239×10−5. The exact value, 2.7496×10−5, lies inside: the upper bound is 5.6% high and the lower bound 0.9% low. Per year the model expects 243.1×2.7496×10−5=0.00668 days, one every 150 years.

  9. A is correct: Φ(−4)=3.17×10−5=0.0032%. B is the two-sided probability of a move of four standard deviations in either direction. C is the one-sided Chebyshev (Cantelli) bound 1/(1+42) of LM14, which holds for every distribution with a finite variance and is far larger.

  10. PV=(1−e−0.02×30)/0.02=22.5594; forever, 1/(0.05−0.03)=50.0. The first 30 years deliver 1−e−0.6=45.1% of the perpetuity's value; LM6 finds almost the same share, 45%, for a discrete perpetuity at a 2% discount rate.

  11. The integrand values are 1, 0.9692332, 0.8824969, 0.7548396 and 0.6065307 at x=0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1. T2​=0.8428811 (error, rule minus exact, −0.0127433), T4​=0.8524588 (error −0.0031656, a ratio of 4.03) and S4​=0.8556513 (error +0.0000269). Simpson's weights 3Δx​(1,4,2,4,1) with Δx=0.25 equal 34​ times the T4​ weights Δx(21​,1,1,1,21​) minus 31​ times the T2​ weights 0.5(21​,0,1,0,21​), so S4​=(4T4​−T2​)/3 identically.

  12. C is correct. By (5.14) the error is proportional to Δx4, and 24=16. A is the trapezoid and midpoint factor.

  13. Mean e0.08+0.02=e0.10=1.1052; median e0.08=1.0833; Pr(G<1)=Pr(lnG<0)=Φ(−0.08/0.20)=Φ(−0.4)=0.3446.

  14. With μ=0, σ=1 and z=−2, (5.11) gives E[Z∣Z≤−2]=−φ(2)/Φ(−2)=−0.05399/0.02275=−2.3732. The large-ω approximation φ(ω)/Q(ω)≈ω+1/ω=2.5 overstates the depth by 5%: at ω=2 the bracket (5.10) is still wide, since 1/ω2=0.25.

  15. Six days: 2020-03-20 (+7.95%), 2022-11-11 (+5.31%), 2024-08-06 (+5.51%), 2025-04-10 (+9.99%), 2026-04-08 (+5.18%) and 2026-07-31 (+10.00%). The normal model expects 2,902×Φ(−3.9668)=0.106 days, so the data hold 57 times as many. The normal model fails in the upper tail too.

  16. The model needs Φ((−0.05−μ^​)/σ)=9/2,902, so (−0.05−μ^​)/σ=−2.7369 and σ=0.050871/2.7369=1.8587%. It then expects 379 days at or below −2% against 104 actual, and 140 at or below −3% against 37.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Riemann sum 黎曼和 ∑i​f(ξi​)Δti​ over a partition; its limit is the integral, (5.1).
Definite integral 定積分 Limit of Riemann sums; accumulated change or signed area.
Antiderivative 反導函數 A function F with F′=f.
Fundamental theorem of calculus 微積分基本定理 dxd​∫ax​f=f(x) and ∫ab​f=F(b)−F(a), (5.2).
Substitution 變數變換 The chain rule read backwards, (5.4).
Integration by parts 分部積分 The product rule read backwards, (5.6).
Improper integral 瑕積分（廣義積分） A limit of integrals, for an unbounded interval or integrand.
Gaussian integral 高斯積分 ∫−∞∞​e−x2/2dx=2π​, (5.7).
Tail index 尾部指數 α in a power tail x−α−1; moments exist below order α.
Kurtosis 峰態 E[(X−μ)4]/σ4: 3 for the normal, infinite if 2<α≤4 (undefined if α≤2); excess kurtosis (超額峰態) subtracts 3.
Continuous annuity 連續年金 Level stream; present value CF0​(1−e−rT)/r.
Duration 存續期間 Present-value-weighted average date; −PV′/PV under continuous compounding.
Probability density 機率密度函數 f≥0 with total area 1; probabilities are areas under it.
Distribution function 累積分布函數 F(x)=Pr(X≤x)=∫−∞x​f; F′=f.
Expectation 期望值 E[h(X)]=∫h(x)f(x)dx, (5.9).
Mills' ratio 米爾斯比率 (1−Φ(ω))/φ(ω); bounds in (5.10).
Conditional tail mean 條件尾端平均 E[R∣R≤κ], (5.11); with κ at the value-at-risk level, minus the expected shortfall (預期短缺) of LM32.
Lognormal 對數常態 G=eX, X normal; mean eμX​+σX2​/2, median eμX​, (5.12).
Trapezoidal rule 梯形法 Chords on each panel; error O(Δx2), (5.13).
Simpson's rule 辛普森法 Parabolas through panel pairs; error O(Δx4), (5.14).
Richardson extrapolation 理查森外插 Combining two step sizes to cancel a known leading error term.
Adaptive quadrature 自適應數值積分 Refining the grid where the estimated error is largest.
